title: Trail Gain
statement: A hiker logs the altitude at each checkpoint of a one-way trail in heights. They want to photograph the biggest climb: start at some checkpoint i and finish at a later checkpoint j, with gain heights[j] - heights[i]. Return the largest gain possible, or 0 if the trail never climbs.

examples.explanation: Start at altitude 1 and finish at 6 for a gain of 5.
The trail only descends, so the best gain is 0.

hints.content: The finish must come after the start.
For a fixed finish j, the best start is the lowest altitude before j.
Keep the lowest altitude seen so far while you walk the trail once.
At each checkpoint, compare its altitude minus the lowest so far with the best gain.
Update the lowest altitude after computing the gain, and start the best gain at 0.

testCases.explanation: Start at altitude 1 and finish at 6 for a gain of 5.
The trail only descends, so the best gain is 0.
Start at the first checkpoint and finish at the last.
8 - 3 = 5 beats 4 - 1 = 3; the lowest point is not always the start.
A large climb after a drop.

solutions.title: Try every start and finish
solutions.intuition: Check every pair with the start before the finish.
solutions.approach: Two nested loops over i < j, tracking the maximum of heights[j] - heights[i] and 0.
solutions.pseudocode: best = 0; for i: for j > i: best = max(best, h[j] - h[i]); return best
commonMistakes: Allowing j < i, which measures a descent backwards.
Starting best at -Infinity and returning a negative gain.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Every start/finish pair is checked, which is correct but quadratic.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Pairs starting at 1 reach 5 - 1 = 4 and 6 - 1 = 5. The best is 5.

solutions.title: Track the lowest point so far
solutions.intuition: The best climb ending at j starts at the minimum altitude before j.
solutions.approach: Walk once. For each height, update best with height - lowest, then update lowest.
solutions.pseudocode: lowest = h[0]; best = 0; for h: best = max(best, h - lowest); lowest = min(lowest, h); return best
commonMistakes: Returning max(heights) - min(heights), which ignores order.
Updating lowest before computing the gain (harmless here, but confusing).
solutions.interviewExplanation: For each finish point the best start is the lowest altitude before it, so I carry that minimum as I scan. That's one pass with constant space. It's the classic 'buy low, sell later' scan.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: At 5: gain 4. At 3: gain 2. At 6: gain 5, so best is 5. At 4: gain 3.
